---
title: "Car Thefts Activity: Code Explainer"
---

This document walks through the key code patterns in the Car Thefts activity, which introduces standard deviation, means, and histograms.

## Loading the tidyverse

```
library(tidyverse)
```

This loads the core collection of R packages you will use in almost every activity. It includes `dplyr` (for data manipulation like `mutate()`, `filter()`, `summarize()`), `ggplot2` (for charts), `readr` (for `read_csv()`), and several others. You only need to load it once per notebook, typically in the first code block.

## Loading a CSV from a URL

```
car_thefts <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/...")
```

`read_csv()` reads a comma-separated values file and turns it into a data frame (a table with rows and columns). You can give it a URL or a local file path. The `<-` arrow saves the result into a variable called `car_thefts` so you can refer to it later.

## Calculating mean and standard deviation with `summarize()`

```
car_thefts |> summarize(mean = mean(count), sd = sd(count))
```

`summarize()` collapses an entire column down to a single summary number. `mean(count)` calculates the average of the `count` column. `sd(count)` calculates the standard deviation. The result is a tiny one-row table with columns named `mean` and `sd`. The pipe `|>` passes `car_thefts` into `summarize()` as its data.

## Creating a histogram

```
car_thefts |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = count), binwidth = 2)
```

`ggplot()` starts a chart. `geom_histogram()` creates a histogram — a bar chart that shows how many values fall into each range (bin). `aes(x = count)` tells it which column to use. `binwidth = 2` means each bar covers a range of 2 units. A narrower binwidth shows more detail; a wider one smooths things out.

## Adding reference lines with `geom_vline()`

```
geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(count)), color = "red", linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +
geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(count) - sd(count)), color = "blue", linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +
geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(count) + sd(count)), color = "blue", linetype = "dashed", size = 1)
```

`geom_vline()` draws a vertical line on the chart. `xintercept` sets where the line goes on the x-axis. Here, three lines are drawn: one at the mean (red) and two at one standard deviation above and below the mean (blue). This visually shows the center and spread of the data.

`linetype = "dashed"` makes the line dashed instead of solid. `size = 1` controls the thickness. You can layer as many `geom_` elements as you want by connecting them with `+`.

## Common mistakes

**Using `read.csv()` instead of `read_csv()`:**

```
# Works, but gives you a base R data frame:
car_thefts <- read.csv("https://...")

# Better — gives you a tibble with cleaner behavior:
car_thefts <- read_csv("https://...")
```

`read_csv()` (with an underscore) is from the tidyverse and is faster, handles column types better, and produces cleaner output. `read.csv()` (with a period) is base R and still works, but you may see unexpected behavior with column names or data types.

**Forgetting to load the tidyverse before using its functions:**

```
# Error: could not find function "read_csv"
car_thefts <- read_csv("https://...")

# Fix: load the library first
library(tidyverse)
car_thefts <- read_csv("https://...")
```

If you see "could not find function," it almost always means you forgot to run the `library()` block.

**Confusing `summarize()` with `mutate()`:**

```
# This gives you a one-row table with just the mean:
car_thefts |> summarize(mean = mean(count))

# This adds a new column to every row, all containing the same mean:
car_thefts |> mutate(mean = mean(count))
```

Use `summarize()` when you want to collapse data down to a summary. Use `mutate()` when you want to add a new column while keeping all the original rows.

**Putting `aes()` outside `geom_histogram()`:**

```
# Wrong — aes() must be inside a geom or inside ggplot():
car_thefts |> ggplot() + geom_histogram(x = count)

# Correct:
car_thefts |> ggplot() + geom_histogram(aes(x = count))
```

The `aes()` wrapper tells ggplot that `count` is a column name, not a fixed value.
